topic: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
title: Mental health law and learning disability
blurb: Apply the Mental Health Act 1983 conduct qualifier for learning disability, tell section 2 from section 3, and describe the 2025 changes that are still to come.
question: Nadia, 24, has a moderate learning disability. Over a week she has stopped eating, appears to respond to voices and has withdrawn. She has never been aggressive or acted irresponsibly. A colleague says she cannot be detained under the Mental Health Act because of her learning disability. Is that right?

teach.h: The 1983 Act, as amended, is the law in force
teach.body: Under the Mental Health Act 1983, mental disorder means any disorder or disability of the mind, so a learning disability can count. The Act defines learning disability as a state of arrested or incomplete development of the mind which includes significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning. In plain English: learning disability is within the Act, but Parliament added an extra safeguard before it can justify longer-term powers.

For section 3 and most longer-term powers, a person with a learning disability is not treated as having a mental disorder by reason of that disability unless it is associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct. The qualifier does not apply to section 2. It also does not stop the Act being used for a separate mental illness, such as depression or psychosis, which is a mental disorder in its own right.

teach.h: Does the qualifier stand in the way?

teach.h: Scenario: Nadia on the assessment ward
teach.body: Nadia, 24, has a moderate learning disability. She has stopped eating, appears to hear voices and has withdrawn, with no aggression. Her colleague is wrong: the qualifier does not apply to section 2, so she can be assessed under section 2 if its criteria are met. If a psychotic illness is diagnosed, that illness is a mental disorder in its own right. The learning disability nurse supports assessment with her communication passport and familiar staff, and rules out physical causes first.

teach.text: Two classic mistakes. First, 'a learning disability means she cannot be sectioned': wrong, because the qualifier does not apply to section 2. Second, 'the 2025 Act has stopped section 3 for learning disability': wrong in October 2026, because that change has not yet come into force.

items: MHA 1983 defines learning disability as arrested or incomplete development of mind with significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning.
For s3, guardianship, CTOs and renewals, LD alone needs abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct.
The qualifier does not apply to s2, or to a separate mental illness.
LD nurses are in the s5(4) prescribed class (up to 6 hours).
MHA 2025: s3 will need a psychiatric disorder, but this is not yet in force.

summary: You can now apply the learning disability conduct qualifier to the right sections, explain why section 2 remains available, and handle physical treatment for detained patients through the MCA. You can also describe the Mental Health Act 2025 changes as coming, not current.

A.q: A student nurse asks what must be present before a learning disability, as a person's only mental disorder, can justify detention for treatment under section 3 of the Mental Health Act 1983. What is the correct answer?
options: A risk of self-neglect at home
Abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct
A diagnosis of a severe or profound learning disability
A previous admission under section 2 of the Act
A.why: MHA 1983 s1(2A)-(2B): for s3 a learning disability counts only if associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct.

whyNot.0: Self-neglect alone does not meet the statutory conduct qualifier.
whyNot.2: Severity of learning disability is not the test; the conduct is.
whyNot.3: A previous section 2 is not a requirement for section 3.

A.q: Nadia, 24, has a moderate learning disability. She has stopped eating, appears to respond to voices and has withdrawn, with no aggressive or irresponsible behaviour. Can she be assessed under section 2 of the Mental Health Act 1983?
options: No, the conduct qualifier blocks every section of the Act
No, she must first be detained under section 5(2)
Yes, but her parents must agree to the application
Yes, the qualifier does not apply to section 2
A.why: The learning disability qualifier in s1(2A)-(2B) does not apply to section 2, so assessment under section 2 is possible if its criteria are met.

whyNot.0: The qualifier covers s3 and other longer-term powers, not section 2.
whyNot.1: Section 5(2) is for informal in-patients and is not a step required before section 2.
whyNot.2: Parental agreement is not needed; an AMHP usually applies, with two medical recommendations.

A.q: In October 2026, a ward manager tells staff that under the Mental Health Act 2025 a person can no longer be detained under section 3 because of a learning disability alone. What is the correct response?
options: The change is in the 2025 Act but is not yet in force
The change came into force when the Act was passed
The change applies to section 2 as well as section 3
The change was removed from the Act before it passed
A.why: The 2025 Act (Royal Assent 18 December 2025) contains this change, but the provisions are prospective and not in force in October 2026. The 1983 Act as amended applies.

whyNot.1: The learning disability and autism provisions did not commence on Royal Assent.
whyNot.2: The 2025 Act does not remove section 2 for people with a learning disability or autistic people; assessment remains possible.
whyNot.3: The change is in the Act as passed; it is simply not yet in force.

B.q: The team is considering guardianship under the Mental Health Act 1983 for Owen, 33. His learning disability is his only mental disorder. Which requirement must be met?
options: Evidence that he has been detained under section 3 before
A learning disability assessed as severe or profound in range
Abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct linked to it
An application made in writing by his nearest relative instead
B.why: Guardianship (s7) is one of the powers covered by the s1(2A)-(2B) qualifier, so the learning disability must be associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct.

whyNot.0: Previous detention is not a requirement for guardianship.
whyNot.1: The qualifier is about conduct, not the severity of the disability.
whyNot.3: An AMHP can make the application; it need not come from the nearest relative.

B.q: Sami, 36, has a mild learning disability and a severe depressive illness with psychotic features. He has no history of aggression. The team believes section 3 may be needed. How does the learning disability qualifier affect this?
options: It prevents section 3 as he has shown no aggressive conduct
It means a court order is needed instead of section 3
It means guardianship must be tried before section 3
It does not apply, as his depression is a mental disorder
B.why: The qualifier applies when the learning disability is the mental disorder relied on. Depression with psychosis is a mental disorder in its own right, so section 3 can be considered on that basis.

whyNot.0: The qualifier does not stop the Act being used for a separate mental illness.
whyNot.1: Section 3 is a civil power; a court order is not needed.
whyNot.2: There is no rule that guardianship must be tried first.

B.q: On an assessment and treatment unit, an informal patient with a learning disability is trying to leave and is at serious risk if he goes. No doctor or approved clinician can attend immediately. Which nurse may use the section 5(4) holding power?
options: A registered adult nurse in charge of the shift
A registered learning disability nurse on the unit
A registered children's nurse covering the unit
A nursing associate with mental health training
B.why: The prescribed class for s5(4) is registered nurses whose field is mental health or learning disabilities. The hold lasts up to 6 hours or until the doctor or approved clinician arrives.

whyNot.0: Adult nurses are not in the prescribed class.
whyNot.2: Children's nurses are not in the prescribed class.
whyNot.3: Nursing associates are not in the prescribed class.

C.q: Ben, 28, has a learning disability and is detained under section 3 on an assessment and treatment unit. He has severe toothache and needs an extraction. He lacks capacity to decide about it. Under which framework should the extraction be given?
options: Part 4 of the Mental Health Act, as he is detained
Consent from his nearest relative on his behalf
The Mental Capacity Act, in his best interests
A second opinion appointed doctor's certificate
C.why: A tooth extraction is physical treatment unrelated to his mental disorder, so Part 4 of the MHA does not cover it. As he lacks capacity, it is given under the MCA in his best interests.

whyNot.0: Part 4 covers treatment for mental disorder, not unrelated physical treatment.
whyNot.1: A nearest relative cannot consent to treatment for an adult.
whyNot.3: A SOAD certifies certain treatments for mental disorder, not dental treatment.

C.q: Jess, 30, has a learning disability and was detained under section 3 because of serious aggression associated with it. After six months of positive behaviour support there has been no aggression for four months. Her section 3 is due for renewal. What must the responsible clinician consider?
options: Renewal follows if she still has a learning disability
Renewal is for 6 months whatever her progress
Renewal needs her nearest relative's written agreement
The conduct qualifier must still be met for renewal
C.why: Renewal under s20 is covered by the s1(2A)-(2B) qualifier, so the learning disability must still be associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct for detention to continue on that basis.

whyNot.0: The disability alone is not enough; the conduct must still be present.
whyNot.1: Renewal depends on the criteria being met, not on a fixed period.
whyNot.2: Renewal is a decision for the responsible clinician, not the nearest relative.

C.q: A learning disability nurse is explaining to families what the Mental Health Act 2025 will change for section 3 once the relevant provisions come into force. Which statement is accurate?
options: Section 3 will need a psychiatric disorder, not LD or autism alone
Section 2 will be closed to people with a learning disability
Section 3 will need a court order for autistic people instead
Section 3 will need the conduct qualifier for autism as well
C.why: The 2025 Act (s3, Sch 1, prospective) will allow section 3 only for psychiatric disorder, so autism or learning disability alone will not justify it. Section 2 stays available for autistic people and people with a learning disability.

whyNot.1: The 2025 Act keeps section 2 available for people with a learning disability; assessment stays possible.
whyNot.2: The Act does not introduce a court order route for section 3.
whyNot.3: The 2025 Act removes autism and learning disability alone as grounds for s3 rather than extending the qualifier.

reteach.title: Ask two questions: which section, and which disorder?
reteach.question: How do you work out whether a person with a learning disability can be detained under a particular section?

blocks.body: First, which section? Section 2 has no learning disability qualifier. Second, which disorder is being relied on? If it is a separate mental illness, the usual criteria apply. If it is the learning disability alone, section 3, guardianship, CTOs and renewals need abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct.

blocks.text: The 2025 Act will end section 3 for learning disability or autism alone, but it is not yet in force. Answer exam questions on the 1983 Act as amended.

explain.body: Learning disability is arrested or incomplete development of the mind with significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning (s1(4)). For longer-term powers, it counts only with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct (s1(2A)-(2B)).

items.label: needed for s3 if LD alone

test.q: How does the Mental Health Act 1983 define learning disability?
options: An IQ below 70 that was identified before the age of 18
Arrested development of mind, impairing intelligence and social functioning
A lifelong condition affecting reading, writing or number skills
A disorder of the mind that needs specialist hospital treatment
test.why: s1(4): a state of arrested or incomplete development of the mind which includes significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning.

whyNot.0: The Act does not define learning disability by an IQ figure.
whyNot.2: Reading or writing difficulties describe a specific learning difficulty, not this definition.
whyNot.3: That is closer to the general idea of mental disorder, not the learning disability definition.

explain.body: Section 2: assessment, up to 28 days, not renewable, no LD qualifier. Section 3: treatment, up to 6 months and renewable, appropriate treatment must be available, qualifier applies if LD is the disorder relied on.

test.q: Which power can be used for a person with a learning disability without the abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct qualifier?
options: Section 3 detention
Section 7 guardianship
A community treatment order
Section 2 detention
test.why: The qualifier in s1(2A)-(2B) does not apply to section 2.

whyNot.0: Section 3 is covered by the qualifier.
whyNot.1: Guardianship is covered by the qualifier.
whyNot.2: CTOs (s17A) are covered by the qualifier.

explain.body: Registered LD and MH nurses are the prescribed class for the s5(4) holding power, up to 6 hours. LD nurses can become AMHPs. Under s145, medical treatment includes habilitation and rehabilitation.

test.q: What is the maximum length of the section 5(4) nurse's holding power?
options: Up to 72 hours
Up to 24 hours
Up to 6 hours
Up to 12 hours
test.why: s5(4): the hold lasts up to 6 hours or until the doctor or approved clinician arrives, whichever is earlier.

whyNot.0: 72 hours is the s5(2) doctor's holding power.
whyNot.1: 24 hours is the s136 place of safety period.
whyNot.3: 12 hours is the possible s136 extension, not s5(4).

explain.body: Royal Assent 18 December 2025. Once in force, s3 will need a psychiatric disorder; autism or learning disability alone will not do. Section 2 stays available for autistic people and people with a learning disability. Care (education) and treatment reviews become statutory. These parts are not yet in force.

test.q: In October 2026, which law governs detention of a person with a learning disability under section 3?
options: The Mental Health Act 2025 alone
The Mental Health Act 1983 as amended
The Mental Capacity Act 2005 Schedule A1
The Care Act 2014 safeguarding duties
test.why: The learning disability and autism provisions of the 2025 Act are not yet in force, so the 1983 Act as amended governs section 3.

whyNot.0: The relevant 2025 provisions are prospective, not in force.
whyNot.2: Schedule A1 is DoLS, which does not authorise detention for treatment of mental disorder.
whyNot.3: The Care Act does not provide powers of detention.
